insider_note: This is the same completing-the-square + √(k²−u²) technique used for a semicircle's area — the answer π(b−a)²/8 is exactly half the area of the circle of diameter (b−a), which is a fast way to sanity-check the final number.

steps.label: Expand the product under the root
steps.margin_note: First two marks. Expand (x−a)(b−x) fully before touching the square root.
steps.memory_tip: (x−a)(b−x) always expands to −x² + (a+b)x − ab — memorise the sign pattern.
lines: Multiply out the product under the root:
(x − a)(b − x) = bx − x² − ab + ax
Collect the x terms: bx + ax = (a + b)x
steps.why: Multiplying out (x−a)(b−x) turns the product of two linear factors into a plain quadratic in x, which can then be handled by completing the square — the standard route to a √(k²−u²) form.
common_mistakes: Losing a sign while expanding, e.g. writing +x² instead of −x².
Expanding only one of the two brackets and leaving the product unexpanded.

steps.label: Complete the square
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. The constant that comes out, (b−a)²/4, is the k² of the standard formula.
steps.memory_tip: The half-sum (a+b)/2 is always the centre of the completed square; the half-difference (b−a)/2 is always the radius k.

lines.text: Take out −1 so that x² has coefficient 1:

steps.why: Completing the square turns the quadratic into a fixed constant minus a squared deviation from the midpoint (a+b)/2, exactly the k² − u² shape the standard root-integral formula needs.
common_mistakes: Making a sign error when pulling the negative sign out of the bracket.
Simplifying ((a+b)/2)² − ab incorrectly instead of reaching (b−a)²/4.

steps.label: Apply the standard √(k² − u²) formula
steps.margin_note: Two marks for correctly identifying k = (b−a)/2 and u = x − (a+b)/2 and applying the formula.
steps.memory_tip: ∫√(k² − u²) du = (u/2)√(k² − u²) + (k²/2) Sin⁻¹(u/k) + c — a formula to have ready for this whole chapter.

lines.text: This is k² − u², a difference of squares:

steps.why: The completed-square form is exactly k² − u² with k = (b−a)/2 fixed and u = x − (a+b)/2 varying, so the standard result for ∫√(k²−u²) du applies directly, ready to be evaluated at the two limits.
common_mistakes: Mixing up which quantity is k (fixed) and which is u (the variable, depending on x).
Forgetting the antiderivative has two terms — dropping the algebraic term and keeping only the Sin⁻¹ term, or vice versa.

steps.label: Evaluate at the limits
steps.margin_note: The last mark. At both endpoints, u = ±k, so √(k²−u²) = 0 and only the Sin⁻¹ terms survive.
steps.memory_tip: At x = b, u = k so Sin⁻¹(1) = π/2; at x = a, u = −k so Sin⁻¹(−1) = −π/2 — the algebraic term vanishes at both ends.
steps.why: At both endpoints the point lies exactly on the boundary of the square-root term (u = ±k), so that term vanishes and only the two Sin⁻¹ terms, which add rather than cancel because Sin⁻¹(−1) = −π/2, are left.
common_mistakes: Wrongly cancelling the two Sin⁻¹ terms instead of adding them.
